title: Management of Female Genital Mutilation Complications

headings.title: Understanding Female Genital Mutilation and Classification
headings.content:
Female Genital Mutilation encompasses all procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Understanding the anatomical classification set by the World Health Organization is essential for planning surgical and nursing interventions.

- **Type I (Clitoridectomy)**: Partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce.
- **Type II (Excision)**: Partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without excision of the labia majora.
- **Type III (Infibulation)**: Narrowing of the vaginal orifice with creation of a covering seal by cutting and apposing the labia minora and/or majora, with or without excision of the clitoris.
- **Type IV (Other)**: All other harmful procedures to the genitalia for non-medical purposes, such as pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, and cauterization.

headings.title: Immediate and Long-Term Clinical Complications
headings.content:
The physical trauma resulting from the procedure manifests in both acute emergencies and chronic health challenges. Healthcare providers must remain vigilant for signs of infection and scarring during routine clinical encounters.

- **Hemorrhage**: Severe bleeding resulting from laceration of the clitoral artery or surrounding vascular structures.
- **Severe Infection**: Acute bacterial invasion leading to pelvic inflammatory disease, tetanus, and sepsis.
- **Chronic Pain**: Persistent neuropathic pain and dyspareunia caused by nerve entrapment within scar tissue.
- **Urological Obstruction**: Retention of urine and recurrent urinary tract infections due to meatal stenosis or anatomical distortion.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Trauma-Informed History Taking
headings.content:
Conducting a physical and social assessment requires a gentle, non-judgmental, and trauma-informed approach. Many women carry profound emotional distress and may feel intensely vulnerable during pelvic examinations. Establishing trust takes precedence over rapid documentation.

The initial consultation should explore urinary habits, menstrual flow dynamics, sexual health concerns, and past obstetric experiences. Clinicians must explain every step of a physical examination before proceeding, offering the patient control and the right to pause or stop the procedure at any time.

headings.title: Surgical Management and Defibulation
headings.content:
Surgical intervention is frequently required for women with Type III infibulation, particularly to relieve obstructive symptoms or prepare for childbirth and sexual intercourse. Defibulation involves surgically opening the scar tissue bridge to restore normal anatomical access to the vagina and urethra.

Timing of defibulation depends on clinical need. It may be performed electively, prior to marriage, or urgently during the first stage of labor. Post-operative care focuses on preventing readhesion of raw wound edges through careful hygiene, gentle separation exercises, and adequate analgesia.

headings.title: Psychological, Psychosexual, and Counseling Support
headings.content:
The psychological impact of female genital mutilation extends far beyond physical healing. Affected women frequently experience anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and profound feelings of incomplete identity or violation. Psychosexual counseling aims to help patients navigate intimacy, address dyspareunia, and reframe their relationship with their bodies.

Multidisciplinary care teams should incorporate mental health specialists who utilize cognitive behavioral therapy and supportive counseling. Normalizing these emotional responses helps reduce isolation and empowers women to seek holistic care.

headings.title: Obstetric and Intrapartum Care
headings.content:
Pregnant women who have undergone female genital mutilation face unique obstetric risks, including prolonged first-stage labor, obstructed labor, fetal distress, and perineal lacerations. Midwives and obstetric nurses must anticipate these challenges during antenatal booking.

Routine birth plans should include provisions for anterior defibulation if the scar tissue impedes fetal descent or prevents adequate vaginal examination. Episiotomies must be performed with caution to avoid compounding existing structural damage, and postpartum hemorrhage protocols should remain readily accessible.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Patient Advocacy
headings.content:
Nurses occupy a frontline position in identifying complications, offering compassionate care, and advocating for affected women within healthcare facilities. Care delivery must remain culturally sensitive while firmly upholding human rights and clinical safety standards.

Advocacy involves educating colleagues against the medicalization of female genital mutilation—the practice of healthcare workers performing the procedure in clinical settings under the mistaken belief that it is safer. Nurses also connect survivors with community support networks and legal resources when requested.

headings.title: Legal Frameworks and Community Education in Nigeria
headings.content:
Eradicating female genital mutilation requires robust legal frameworks combined with grassroots community engagement, particularly across regions in Nigeria where traditional practices run deep. The Violence Against Persons Prohibition Act provides a federal legal basis prohibiting the practice, supported by various state-level legislation.

Healthcare professionals play a vital role in community education by engaging traditional birth attendants, religious leaders, and youth groups. Dialogue must focus on shifting cultural norms by promoting alternative rites of passage that celebrate community entry without causing bodily harm.
